docs.title: OpenEnergy
docs.text:
OpenEnergy backtests battery storage and renewable plants against real day-ahead power prices. You describe the assets and a forecasting approach in a short YAML file; OpenEnergy plans each day on the forecast, settles the plan at the prices that actually cleared, and tells you what the site earned, how hard the battery worked, and how close it came to a perfect-foresight benchmark.

It is built for research questions such as:

  • How much is a 2-hour battery worth in the GB day-ahead market?
  • How much more does it earn selling frequency response too?
  • How much revenue does a better price forecast buy?
  • How much of the average price do solar and wind actually capture?
  • Can a battery share a solar farm's grid connection without losing money?
  • As wind and solar grow, how much surplus appears, and how much storage absorbs it?
  • What do storage and renewables do to emissions, and what does a carbon price change?
  • How well does a cost-based model of GB plants reproduce real prices, and what changes with more wind, more storage or a different carbon price?
  • What might GB prices and a battery look like on NESO's Future Energy Scenarios, with interconnectors trading at neighbouring markets' prices?

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/koulakhilesh/OpenEnergy.git
cd OpenEnergy
uv sync --extra forecast
uv run openenergy compare examples/gb-2019-{naive,ml,perfect}.yaml

scenario         forecast             days       revenue   per MW-yr   capture   cycles
gb-2019-perfect  perfect_foresight     363        19,075      19,180    100.0%      464
gb-2019-ml       gradient_boosting     363        14,086      14,164     73.8%      400
gb-2019-naive    naive_last_week       363        13,918      13,995     73.0%      465

A 1 MW / 2 MWh battery trading GB day-ahead prices in 2019 would have earned about £14k per MW-year planning on last week's prices, or 73% of what perfect foresight allows.

The same battery on every year of the bundled prices (examples/gb-2022-naive.yaml with other dates; Ember prices, GBP per MW-year):

Year 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 Last week's prices 20,682 18,889 13,936 17,155 74,172 76,940 35,964 28,677 35,861 Perfect foresight 26,252 25,380 19,538 22,362 89,282 102,550 45,968 38,870 44,564 Capture 79% 74% 71% 77% 83% 75% 78% 74% 80%

Revenue followed the gas crisis: over five times the 2019 level in 2021–2022, and two to two and a half times it in 2023–2025, while a simple forecast kept 71–83% of the perfect-foresight value every year.

Renewables are one command away:

uv run openenergy capture data/time_series/time_series_60min_singleindex_filtered.csv -t solar

GB solar captured 94–106% of the average day-ahead price each year from 2015 to 2019, and adding a 5 MW battery behind an existing 10 MW solar connection cost almost nothing in lost trading (see Research).

The whole system is one command too:

uv run openenergy netload data/time_series/time_series_60min_singleindex_filtered.csv \
  --scale-wind 3 --scale-solar 3 --must-run 8000

Tripling 2019 wind and solar would leave 14 TWh of surplus above an 8 GW must-run floor; a 10 GW / 24 h storage fleet absorbs about three-quarters of it (see System analysis).

And the plants behind the price:

uv run openenergy system validate

Rebuilt from fuel, carbon and fleet data alone, GB's 2019 average price comes out at £42.3/MWh against £42.9 actual, but its peaks are far too low: a battery that earned £16k per MW-year on real 2019 prices earns almost nothing on the modelled ones (see System model).

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
1. Loads prices, capacity factors, demand and carbon intensity from the bundled Open Power System Data, Ember and NESO extracts (GB prices to October 2026) and checks them: UTC timestamps, a regular grid, reported gaps and filtered telemetry glitches.
  2. Forecasts each day using only data available at the decision time (noon the day before by default).
  3. Plans the day with a mixed-integer optimisation that respects power and energy limits, efficiencies, an end-of-day state of charge and, for co-located sites, a shared grid connection; an optional carbon price steers dispatch.
  4. Settles the plan at actual prices through the battery physics, including cycle and calendar ageing.
  5. Reports revenue, cycles, state of health, forecast error, the capture ratio against perfect foresight, net emissions and, for sites, curtailment, the plant's captured price and the value of co-location against separate connections.
  6. Analyses the system: net load, ramps and surplus as renewables scale, and the storage needed to absorb that surplus; openenergy sweep sizes storage for a site.
  7. Models GB dispatch: CCGT, coal and peaking plant in merit order from DUKES fleet data, fuel and carbon prices, checked against 2015–2025, with scenarios for renewables, storage, fleet and carbon policy (storage via the optional PyPSA backend), and optional unit commitment with start-up costs and minimum stable output.
  8. Reports any saved run, system scenario, backcast or sweep as one interactive HTML page of charts and tables (openenergy report; see the example).
  9. Stacks revenue: GB Dynamic Containment, Moderation and Regulation co-optimised with day-ahead trading in the same plan, with the energy each service moves taken from GB frequency data (see Revenue stacking).
  10. Looks forward: NESO Future Energy Scenarios pathways to 2035 on a historic weather year, with GB's interconnectors as price-taking links to six neighbouring markets at availabilities fitted from their actual flows, and unit commitment (see Forward scenarios).
  11. Runs in the browser: a web app (React front end on a FastAPI JSON API) values a battery on any GB year from 2017 or on a FES pathway; try it at open-energy-eight.vercel.app.

See Concepts for the equations and Scenarios for every setting.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Released

Release Scope v2.0 Battery arbitrage backtesting: physics, ageing, dispatch, forecasters, CLI v2.1 PV and wind assets, captured price, co-located storage v2.2 Net load, surplus, storage sizing, emissions v3.0 GB system dispatch with conventional generation via PyPSA, checked against 2015–2020 v3.1 Optional unit commitment (start-up costs, minimum stable output) and a start-cost price, re-checked against 2015–2020 without fitting to prices v3.2 Data to 2025: GB prices from Ember, NESO generation and carbon intensity, DUKES and fuel prices, UK ETS; openenergy data update; backcast of the gas crisis and coal exit v3.3 Multi-day planning horizon (dispatch.lookahead_days), and a measured answer on planning under price uncertainty: for day-ahead-only trading a scenario plan equals one forecast, and risk aversion costs revenue v3.4 Reports: openenergy report turns saved runs, system scenarios, backcasts and sweeps into one interactive HTML file; chart functions reusable from Python v3.5 Revenue stacking: GB Dynamic Containment, Moderation and Regulation co-optimised with day-ahead trading; a measured answer on balancing (imbalance prices are valuable only with a forecast open data does not give) and on stochastic planning (still no value) v4.0 Forward scenarios from NESO's Future Energy Scenarios on a historic weather year; GB's interconnectors as price-taking links to six neighbouring markets, checked against actual flows 2019–2025; a web app (FastAPI, Vercel) valuing a battery on history or a FES pathway v4.1 A usable web app: the answer first in plain words, instant results for common batteries, value by year and by FES pathway at a glance, side-by-side comparison with shareable links, explanations next to each term, CSV and scenario downloads, and a JSON API; CITATION.cff and PyPI release v4.2 A more credible model: unit commitment with interconnector links; each link's availability fitted from its actual flows, never from prices; a measured answer on the missing daily spread (the everyday intraday shape, not negative prices); forward scenarios and the app re-run. GB zones were dropped: GB keeps one national wholesale price (DESNZ, REMA summer update, July 2025) v5.0 A React and TypeScript front end on an extended JSON API (options, explore, compare, FES table), typed from the OpenAPI schema and tested end to end; interconnector availability by price gap from hourly flows, tested out of sample (an option: it does not beat the flat share); data refreshed to October 2026; versioned docs and a Zenodo DOI (current)

Planned

Release Scope v5.1 Model follow-ups: why the modelled 2021–2022 gas-crisis spread is only 27–39% of actual; constraints between Scotland and England and the curtailment they cause; a better day-ahead plan than last week's prices

Alongside releases: refresh and re-check the bundled data every release; keep CI and its actions current; revisit stochastic planning if an open, forecastable market price appears. Ideas are welcome in issues.

docs.title: availability_from_flows
docs.text:
availability_from_flows(system_dir, gb_prices, neighbours)

Per link, the share of a price taker's imports and exports that actually flowed.

A price taker on gb_prices (actual hourly GBP/MWh, the fitting years) imports at full capacity whenever GB is dearer than the neighbour and exports whenever it is cheaper, from the day the link entered service. Each share is the actual energy (Elexon) over that trade, at most 1. Modelled prices are never used. Links with no trade in the period get the mean of the others.

docs.title: availability_by_gap
docs.text:
availability_by_gap(system_dir, gb_prices, neighbours)

Per link and direction, the share of capacity used by size of the price gap.

Hours from the day each link entered service are binned by the gap between gb_prices (actual hourly GBP/MWh) and the neighbour's actual price, from the lower edges in GAP_EDGES: imports when GB is dearer, exports when cheaper. Each bin's share is the link's mean hourly flow that way (Elexon, hourly) over its capacity, made non-decreasing in the gap (weighted by hours) so that it can be offered as stepped capacity. Bins without hours take their neighbour's share. Modelled prices are never used. Columns: link, direction, gap_from, share, hours.

docs.title: openenergy.dispatch.arbitrage
docs.text: Single-battery energy arbitrage as a mixed-integer linear programme (HiGHS).

docs.title: DispatchConfig dataclass
docs.text:
Optimisation settings.

end_soc is a fraction of usable energy; None means return to the starting energy. max_cycles caps equivalent full cycles over the horizon (the backtest scales it by the days planned, so it stays a per-day cap). lookahead_days makes the backtest plan each day together with that many following days of forecasts, settling only the first; the end-energy target then applies at the end of the last day.

docs.title: DispatchPlan dataclass
docs.text:
Optimal schedule in MW per interval and stored energy at each boundary (T+1).

With frequency response, reserve_mw is MW held per block and service, and response_charge_mw/response_discharge_mw the expected average power it moves. expected_revenue covers energy; expected_response the availability payments.

docs.title: Reserve dataclass
docs.text:
Frequency-response options over a horizon.

block maps each interval to a row of price (-1 where nothing can be reserved). price (GBP/MW/h) and utilisation (MWh delivered per MW per hour) have one row per block and one column per service. fixed holds MW already committed (NaN where free). beyond_hours is how long each block runs past the horizon end; the plan keeps enough energy to stay idle through it. With energy_paid, delivered energy is bought or sold at the interval's price; otherwise it is free, as under NESO's ABSVD adjustment.

make_features(index, prices, lead_hours)

Calendar and lagged-price features; lags at or after the decision time are NaN.

docs.title: openenergy.backtest.engine
docs.text: Rolling day-ahead backtest: plan on forecasts, settle at actual prices.

docs.title: BacktestConfig dataclass
docs.text: lead_hours: how long before each UTC day the plan is fixed (12 = noon the day before).

docs.title: Site dataclass
docs.text:
Renewable output (MW, on the price grid) sharing grid with the battery.

Output is known when planning (perfect generation foresight).

docs.title: Carbon dataclass
docs.text:
Actual grid carbon intensity (gCO2/kWh) for accounting and, with a price, for dispatch.

planning sets what dispatch sees: last_week uses the same interval a week earlier (two weeks if missing), cut off at the decision time like prices; actual uses the real values and is an upper bound. NESO's archived "forecast" is not used: it is the last forecast before each half-hour, so planning on it the day before would look ahead. Reported money stays market revenue.

docs.title: run_backtest
docs.text:
run_backtest(
    spec,
    prices,
    forecaster,
    config=None,
    days=None,
    site=None,
    carbon=None,
    response=None,
)

Simulate each UTC day in order; the battery ages through every calendar day in range.

With a site, the battery shares a grid connection with renewable output. With carbon, emissions are reported and a carbon price steers dispatch. With response, frequency-response availability is sold alongside trading.

docs.title: Time and units
docs.text: Prices are a series on a regular UTC grid; each timestamp labels the start of its interval of length \(\Delta t\) hours. Power is in MW, energy in MWh and prices in currency per MWh. Days are UTC days.

docs.title: Battery physics
docs.text:
A battery has a power rating \(P\) (MW), a rated energy \(E_{rated}\) (MWh), charge and discharge efficiencies \(\eta_c, \eta_d\), and a state-of-charge window \([SOC_{min}, SOC_{max}]\) expressed as fractions of usable energy.

For charge \(c_t\) and discharge \(d_t\) (MW) in interval \(t\), stored energy evolves as

\[E_{t+1} = E_t + \eta_c\, c_t\, \Delta t - \frac{d_t\, \Delta t}{\eta_d}\]

Each interval adds its own throughput to the equivalent full cycle count:

\[N \mathrel{+}= \frac{(c_t + d_t)\,\Delta t}{2 E_{rated}}\]

State of health is computed from lifetime totals, so it never compounds:

\[SOH = 1 - k_{cycle}\, N - k_{calendar}\, \text{age in years}\]

Usable energy is \(E_{rated} \cdot SOH\). Ageing is applied at the end of every UTC day, including days that are not simulated.

docs.title: Dispatch
docs.text:
Each day is planned by maximising forecast revenue less an optional degradation cost \(\kappa\) per MWh of throughput:

\[\max \sum_t \hat p_t\, (d_t - c_t)\, \Delta t - \kappa \sum_t (c_t + d_t)\, \Delta t\]

With a carbon price \(\lambda\) (currency per tCO2), the planning price becomes \(\hat p_t + \lambda \hat e_t / 1000\) for planned carbon intensity \(\hat e_t\) in gCO2/kWh, so importing is dearer and exporting worth more when the grid is carbon-intensive. Reported revenue stays at market prices; see System analysis.

subject to the energy balance above for \(t = 0 \dots T-1\) with \(E_0\) fixed, and:

  • \(0 \le c_t \le P\, u_t\) and \(0 \le d_t \le P\,(1 - u_t)\) with \(u_t \in \{0, 1\}\), so the battery never charges and discharges at once (an LP would, to burn energy at negative prices);
  • \(SOC_{min}\, E_{usable} \le E_t \le SOC_{max}\, E_{usable}\);
  • \(E_T \ge E_{target}\), by default the energy the day started with;
  • optionally, \(\sum_t (c_t + d_t)\, \Delta t \le 2 N_{max}\, E_{usable}\).

The model is solved with HiGHS; a day takes a few milliseconds.

docs.title: Backtest timing
docs.text:
For each day \(D\):

  1. The forecaster receives prices strictly before the decision time, lead_hours before the start of \(D\) (default 12, i.e. noon on \(D-1\)).
  2. The optimiser plans \(D\) on the forecast, together with the next lookahead_days days of forecasts if set (all made at the same decision time); the end-energy target then applies at the end of the last planned day.
  3. Only \(D\)'s part of the plan is applied through the battery physics and valued at actual prices.
  4. The battery state carries into \(D+1\), which is planned afresh.

Near the end of the data, or before a gap, the lookahead shortens to the days that can be forecast. With lookahead_days: 0 (the default) each day is planned alone and must end with the energy it started with.

Days with missing prices, or for which the forecaster has no usable history, are skipped and listed with the reason. Scenarios that are not perfect foresight also run a perfect-foresight benchmark on the same days.

docs.title: Forecasters
docs.text:
Method Description perfect_foresight The actual prices; the upper bound. naive_last_week The same interval seven days earlier, falling back to fourteen. noisy_foresight Actual prices plus seeded Gaussian error of a chosen spread. gradient_boosting Gradient-boosted trees on calendar features and 1/2/7/14-day lags (needs the forecast extra).

The gradient-boosting model masks any lag at or after the decision time in exactly the same way during training and forecasting, and is trained only on a window that ends before the backtest starts.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text: Metric Definition Revenue \(\sum_t p_t\,(d_t - c_t)\,\Delta t\) at actual prices Revenue per MW-year Revenue \(/\,P \times 365\,/\) days simulated Captured spread Revenue per MWh discharged Equivalent cycles Lifetime \(N\) at the end of the run Forecast MAE / RMSE Error of the forecast against actual prices Capture ratio Revenue / perfect-foresight revenue on common days

docs.title: Renewable plants
docs.text:
A plant has a technology, an installed capacity \(C\) and an annual degradation rate \(r\). Its available output follows the OPSD capacity factor \(cf_t\):

\[g_t = C \cdot cf_t \cdot (1 - r)^{\text{age}}\]

docs.title: Captured price
docs.text:
The captured price is what the market paid per MWh the plant actually produced; the capture rate compares it with the time-weighted (baseload) average:

\[\bar p_{cap} = \frac{\sum_t p_t\, g_t}{\sum_t g_t} \qquad \text{capture rate} = \frac{\bar p_{cap}}{\frac{1}{T}\sum_t p_t}\]

A capture rate below 100% means the technology tends to produce when prices are low; falling capture rates as a technology's share grows are known as cannibalisation. openenergy capture reports this per year, together with capacity factor and the share of output produced at negative prices.

docs.title: Co-located sites
docs.text:
A plant and a battery can share one grid connection with an export limit \(X\), an import limit \(I\) and an optional premium \(\pi\) per MWh of renewable output delivered (ROC- or CfD-like support).

flowchart LR
    G[Plant output] -->|y| Grid
    G -->|s| B[Battery]
    G -->|k| C[Curtailed]
    Grid -->|m| B
    B -->|d| Grid

Each interval, output \(G_t = y_t + s_t + k_t\) goes to the grid, to the battery, or is curtailed; the battery charges \(c_t = s_t + m_t\) from the plant and the grid (\(m_t \le I\)), and net export \(x_t = y_t + d_t - m_t \le X\). The daily plan maximises

\[\sum_t \left[\hat p_t\, x_t + \pi\,(y_t + s_t)\right]\Delta t - \kappa \sum_t (c_t + d_t)\,\Delta t\]

with the battery constraints above. Output is curtailed when the price falls below \(-\pi\) or the connection is full and the battery cannot absorb it.

Every site run is compared with the same plant and battery on separate connections: the plant exports up to its own capacity and the battery trades on its own. The difference is the co-location value; it is negative when a shared connection is too small, and should be weighed against the connection capacity saved.

Upper bound

Plans use the actual plant output (perfect generation foresight) and forecast prices. Co-location results are therefore an upper bound.

docs.title: Bundled extract
docs.text:
data/time_series/time_series_60min_singleindex_filtered.csv is an hourly extract of the Open Power System Data time-series package covering Great Britain from 31 December 2014 to 30 September 2020. It contains the GB day-ahead price (in GBP/MWh), load, and solar and wind generation and capacity. Timestamps are UTC (utc_timestamp). Version 2020-10-06 is still OPSD's latest time-series release (checked 13 October 2026), so later years come from the sources below.

Of 2,101 days, 2,085 have a complete set of prices. The gaps are two-hour holes on the spring clock change each year, two single missing hours, and four outages of about a day. With the default max_gap_hours: 2, the short gaps are interpolated and the outages are skipped.

Prices include genuine scarcity spikes, up to £999/MWh in September–November 2016; they are kept.

docs.title: GB prices after 2020
docs.text:
OPSD's GB prices stop in September 2020. data/prices/gb_day_ahead_ember.csv carries the GB hourly day-ahead price from 30 June 2016 to 28 October 2026 (90,553 hours, no gaps), from Ember's European wholesale price data (CC BY 4.0), stored in EUR/MWh as published. OpenEnergy converts each hour to GBP at the ECB reference rate for its day (data/prices/ecb_gbp_per_eur.csv; the latest earlier rate on weekends and holidays). Use it with data: {source: ember, path: ...}; openenergy data update downloads the latest months into a user cache.

Where both exist (July 2016 to September 2020, 37,239 hours) the converted Ember price matches OPSD with correlation 0.99996 and a mean absolute difference of £0.11/MWh, so the two can be joined. The system model's backcast does exactly that: OPSD where it has a price, Ember otherwise.

Year 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 Mean £/MWh 45.3 57.4 42.9 35.3 117.8 204.8 94.1 72.5 80.7 Mean daily spread £/MWh 41.6 40.6 32.9 39.6 146.4 155.6 70.0 59.9 67.5

The series keeps 615 negative hours (down to −€60/MWh) and 38 hours at €1,000/MWh or more (up to €2,576/MWh in 2021–2022). From 2021 Ember takes the UK price from EMR Settlement, whose own reuse terms could not be read (the site blocks scripted access); OpenEnergy relies on Ember's CC BY 4.0 publication and cites both.

docs.title: Neighbouring markets
docs.text:
data/prices/europe_day_ahead_ember.csv holds the hourly day-ahead prices of the six markets GB's interconnectors reach (France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Norway, Denmark and Ireland), EUR/MWh as published by Ember, from 1 January 2015 (Ireland from 1 October 2018) to 30 October 2026. The system model's interconnector links trade at these prices, converted to GBP like the GB price.

Mean £/MWh (ECB rates) 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 GB 42.9 35.3 117.8 204.8 94.1 72.5 80.7 France 34.6 28.7 93.4 235.1 84.4 48.9 52.2 Netherlands 36.1 28.7 88.1 206.2 83.5 65.3 74.3 Belgium 34.5 28.4 89.1 208.4 84.7 59.4 70.6 Norway 34.2 8.2 53.6 118.8 51.5 32.8 40.9 Denmark 34.2 23.5 75.4 184.0 73.7 59.8 69.9 Ireland 44.2 33.5 116.3 192.5 110.0 92.0 97.8

From 2023 to 2025 GB's mean price was above every neighbour's except Ireland's, which helps explain why price-taking links at full capacity import so much (each link's availability is therefore fitted from its flows; see below).

Known issues: Ember publishes one price for Norway and one for Denmark, without saying how the bidding zones are combined; GB's links land in southern Norway (NO2) and western Denmark (DK1). A few hours are blank on 31 July and 30 September 2026 (none before 2026).

docs.title: Renewable capacity factors
docs.text:
The extract also has hourly capacity-factor profiles (generation divided by installed capacity) for solar, wind, wind_onshore and wind_offshore, from 2015 to 29 December 2019; OPSD stops publishing capacity after that.

In 233 hours the solar profile exceeds 1.0 (up to 1.367): reported capacity lags new build, so generation divided by capacity overshoots. OpenEnergy clips profiles to [0, 1] and reports how many values were clipped. The same lag pushes GB solar capacity factors to 15–18%, above the roughly 11% usually quoted; this changes absolute output but not capture rates, which depend on the shape of the profile.

Other OPSD zones can be used by pointing data.path at a larger OPSD time_series_*_singleindex.csv. OPSD publishes GB prices in GBP and all other zones in EUR; OpenEnergy labels the currency accordingly.

docs.title: Carbon intensity
docs.text:
data/carbon_intensity/gb_national.csv holds GB national carbon intensity for every half-hour from 1 January 2018 to 29 October 2026: NESO's forecast and its estimated actual, in gCO2/kWh. It was downloaded with scripts/fetch_carbon_intensity.py and is stored exactly as published; 179 half-hours the API did not return are left blank.

The archive has 804 half-hours without an actual value (18 runs, the longest about three days) and 16 implausible forecasts (up to 13,579 gCO2/kWh). OpenEnergy treats any value outside 0–1000 gCO2/kWh as missing and reports how many it rejected. Annual mean actual intensity falls from 248 (2018) to 214 (2019), 180 (2020), 188 (2021), 183 (2022), 152 (2023), 125 (2024), 129 (2025) and 122 gCO2/kWh (2026 to 12 October).

These are average intensities of the whole system. Storage and renewables change the marginal plant, whose emissions can differ; emissions results in OpenEnergy show direction and rough scale, not causal impact.

docs.title: GB system data
docs.text:
data/system/, written by scripts/fetch_system_data.py, feeds the system model:

File Contents Source generation_mix.csv Half-hourly GB generation by fuel, MW, 2015-01-01 to 2025-12-31 (192,864 rows, no gaps) NESO historic generation mix fleet.csv GB capacity at each year end 2014–2025 (CCGT, coal, gas turbines, oil engines, nuclear, pumped storage) and CCGT and coal efficiency DUKES 5.8 and 5.10 fuel_prices.csv Quarterly coal, oil and gas prices paid by major power producers, 2014–2025 DESNZ QEP 3.2.1 carbon_prices.csv EU ETS (2015–2020) and UK ETS (2021–2025) price on 1 April with ECB exchange rates, and carbon price support rates World Bank, DESNZ (2021), ECB, HMRC unit_parameters.csv Unit size, minimum stable output and start-up cost for CCGT, coal and peaking plant (unit commitment) Danish Energy Agency, NREL, ECB interconnectors.csv GB's ten built interconnectors: neighbour, import and export capacity (MW) NESO Interconnector Register, 12 October 2026 interconnector_flows.csv Daily imports and exports per link, MWh, 2016-01-01 to 2026-10-29 Elexon BMRS FUELHH interconnector_flows_hourly.csv Hourly net flow per link, MW, 2019-01-01 to 2026-10-29 Elexon BMRS FUELHH interconnector_availability.csv Each link's import and export availability: actual flow over a price taker's trade on actual prices, 2019–2025 Elexon BMRS FUELHH, Ember, OPSD, ECB interconnector_gap_availability.csv Each link's share of capacity used by size of the price gap (option availability: gap), 2019–2025 Elexon BMRS FUELHH, Ember, OPSD, ECB

The model's inputs stop at the latest complete calendar year, 2025 (checked 13 October 2026): DUKES publishes a year's fleet the following July, so 2026 has none yet, and the 2026 fuel and carbon prices that exist are not added until the year is complete, so every model year has the same kind of inputs.

Known issues: NESO fills gaps by seasonal decomposition and sets net-negative values to zero, so pumping demand and net exports are absent; transmission solar and batteries are in "other". DUKES efficiencies are UK-wide averages. One ETS price per year misses moves within the year (EU ETS 2018 rose from about €10 to €25; UK ETS 2021–2023 swung more). The World Bank dashboard has no UK ETS price on 1 April 2021, before the first auction, so 2021 uses DESNZ's 2021 carbon price (mean auction price, £47.96/t). DESNZ suppresses some coal prices from 2023 (carried forward) and gives no coal efficiency for 2025 (latest earlier value used). Fuel prices are what power producers paid, including contracts agreed earlier, so they lag market gas prices: see the system model. Emission factors (gas 0.1839, coal 0.3096 tCO2 per MWh of fuel) follow from the carbon price support rates, which are set at £18/tCO2.

The interconnector register holds today's capacities only. Each link's first day in service comes from its flows (the first flow in the first 14 days carrying at least a fifth of its capacity, which skips commissioning tests): Nemo Link 2019-01-30, IFA2 2021-01-22, NS Link 2021-09-23, ElecLink 2022-05-23, Viking Link 2023-12-29 and Greenlink 2025-01-19. The flows also show limits the register does not (Moyle about 300 MW in 2016–2017, IFA about half its capacity in 2022, BritNed never above about 1,050 of 1,200 MW), so modelled link capacity is overstated in those periods.

Each link's availability (scripts/fit_interconnector_availability.py) is the energy it actually moved (Elexon) over what a price taker would have moved at full capacity on actual GB and neighbour day-ahead prices, per direction, capped at 1. It uses actual prices and flows only. Fitted on 2019–2022 it gives 36.9 TWh of imports in 2024 (actual 43.9, full capacity 66.0) and 11.8 TWh of exports (actual 10.6); the published file is fitted on 2019–2025.

docs.title: Future Energy Scenarios
docs.text:
data/fes/ holds NESO's Future Energy Scenarios tables unchanged, written by scripts/fetch_fes.py: the electricity supply (ES1) and demand summary (ED1) tables of FES: Pathways to Net Zero 2025 (pathways Holistic Transition, Electric Engagement, Hydrogen Evolution and Falling Behind, plus the Ten Year Forecast; 2024–2050) and of the 2026 Ten Year Outlook (2025–2036). system.fes uses their capacities (MW), storage (GWh) and annual system demand; see forward scenarios. FES 2025's 2025 column is already a projection and differs by pathway; FES publishes no fuel or carbon prices and no storage efficiencies.

data/scenarios/ is model output, not source data: hourly modelled prices for each pathway in 2030 and 2035 on 2025's weather (fes_prices.csv) and a summary next to FES's own figures (fes_summary.csv), written by scripts/build_scenario_prices.py for the web app. data/app/ is model output too: per-MW battery results for common requests (1, 2 and 4 hours, every year, response option and pathway), written by scripts/build_app_results.py so the app answers at once.

docs.title: Frequency response
docs.text:
data/response/, written by scripts/fetch_response_data.py, feeds revenue stacking:

  • gb_dynamic_response.csv: the clearing price (GBP/MW/h) and cleared volume (MW) of each dynamic response service (DC, DM, DR; low and high) for every four-hour EFA block from 15 September 2021 22:00 to 30 October 2026 19:00 UTC (11,226 blocks, no gaps). DM and DR start on 26 March 2022.
  • gb_response_utilisation.csv: for each month from September 2021 to September 2026, the average share of contracted MW each service delivers (MWh per MW per hour), from NESO's one-second GB frequency and the delivery envelopes in NESO's Response Services Service Terms (version 6). The raw frequency files (about 75 MB a month) are not bundled.

Known issues: Dynamic Containment before 16 September 2021 was bought pay-as-bid and is not included; some prices are negative (mostly DM and DR high); utilisation is the delivery of a unit following the envelope exactly. See data/response/README.md.

docs.title: Imbalance prices
docs.text: data/balancing/gb_system_prices.csv, written by scripts/fetch_system_prices.py, holds the GB system (imbalance) price for every half-hour from 2016 to 29 October 2026 (189,840 periods, 20 blank where Elexon's API returned nothing). GB has a single imbalance price, so the sell and buy prices are equal; it is used by examples/imbalance_value.py.

docs.title: Attribution
docs.text:
Prices, load and renewables

Open Power System Data. 2020. Data Package Time series. Version 2020-10-06. https://doi.org/10.25832/time_series/2020-10-06. (Primary data from various sources, for a complete list see URL).

The primary price and load data come from the ENTSO-E Transparency Platform.

Carbon intensity

National Energy System Operator (NESO). Carbon Intensity API. https://carbonintensity.org.uk/. Licensed under CC BY 4.0; terms of use.

OpenEnergy treats out-of-range values as missing and averages half-hours to the analysis step; the bundled file itself is unchanged.

Generation mix

National Energy System Operator (NESO). Historic generation mix and carbon intensity. https://www.neso.energy/data-portal/historic-generation-mix (accessed 10 October 2026). Licensed under the NESO Open Data Licence v1.0. Supported by National Energy SO Open Data.

Fleet capacity and efficiency

Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. Digest of UK Energy Statistics (DUKES) 2026, Chapter 5: table 5.8 (major power producers plant capacity, England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland) and table 5.10 (plant loads, demand and efficiency). https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/electricity-chapter-5-digest-of-united-kingdom-energy-statistics-dukes (accessed 10 October 2026).

Fuel prices

Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. Quarterly Energy Prices, table 3.2.1: average prices of fuels purchased by the major UK power producers. https://www.gov.uk/government/statistical-data-sets/prices-of-fuels-purchased-by-major-power-producers (accessed 10 October 2026).

Carbon price support

HM Revenue & Customs. Excise Notice CCL1/6: a guide to carbon price floor, section 2.3, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/excise-notice-ccl16-a-guide-to-carbon-price-floor, and Climate Change Levy rates, https://www.gov.uk/guidance/climate-change-levy-rates (both accessed 10 October 2026).

UK ETS price for 2021

Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (UK ETS Authority). UK ETS: carbon prices for use in civil penalties, 2021 and 2022. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/determinations-of-the-uk-ets-carbon-price (accessed 10 October 2026).

The four UK government sources contain public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

EU ETS and UK ETS prices

World Bank. Carbon Pricing Dashboard: price of EU ETS (2015–2020) and UK ETS (2022–2025) allowances on 1 April each year. https://carbonpricingdashboard.worldbank.org/compliance/price (accessed 10 October 2026). Licensed under CC BY 4.0.

GB prices after 2020

Ember. European Wholesale Electricity Price Data, hourly, United Kingdom. https://ember-energy.org/data/european-wholesale-electricity-price-data/ (accessed 30 October 2026). Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Primary sources: ENTSO-E Transparency Platform and EMR Settlement.

OpenEnergy keeps Ember's EUR prices unchanged and converts them to GBP with ECB daily rates.

Neighbouring day-ahead prices

Ember. European Wholesale Electricity Price Data, hourly, France, Netherlands, Belgium, Norway, Denmark and Ireland. https://ember-energy.org/data/european-wholesale-electricity-price-data/ (accessed 30 October 2026). Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Primary sources: ENTSO-E Transparency Platform and SEMOpx (Ireland).

Interconnectors

National Energy System Operator (NESO). Interconnector Register (12 October 2026). https://www.neso.energy/data-portal/interconnector-register (accessed 13 October 2026). Licensed under the NESO Open Data Licence v1.0. Supported by National Energy SO Open Data.

Elexon. BMRS Insights API, generation by fuel type (FUELHH), interconnector flows, https://bmrs.elexon.co.uk/ (accessed 30 October 2026). Reused under the BMRS data licence. Contains BMRS data © Elexon Limited copyright and database right 2026.

Future Energy Scenarios

National Energy System Operator (NESO). FES: Pathways to Net Zero 2025 and 2026 Ten Year Outlook: Electricity Supply Data Table (ES1), https://www.neso.energy/data-portal/future-energy-scenario-electricity-supply-data-table-es1, and Electricity Demand Summary (ED1), https://www.neso.energy/data-portal/fes-electricity-demand-summary-data-table-ed1 (accessed 13 October 2026). Licensed under the NESO Open Data Licence v1.0. Supported by National Energy SO Open Data.

Exchange rates

Source: European Central Bank, euro foreign exchange reference rates for GBP and USD. https://data.ecb.europa.eu/ (accessed 10 October 2026; daily GBP rates refreshed 30 October 2026).

OpenEnergy derives a USD-to-GBP cross rate from the two ECB rates to convert the World Bank's US$ prices, and uses the daily GBP rate to convert Ember's EUR prices; the stored rates are unchanged.

Frequency response

National Energy System Operator (NESO). Dynamic Containment, Regulation and Moderation auction results, https://www.neso.energy/data-portal/dynamic-containment-data; Enduring Auction Capability (EAC) auction results, https://www.neso.energy/data-portal/eac-auction-results; System frequency data, https://www.neso.energy/data-portal/system-frequency-data (all accessed 30 October 2026). Licensed under the NESO Open Data Licence v1.0. Supported by National Energy SO Open Data.

Delivery envelopes: NESO, Response Services Service Terms, version 6 (https://www.neso.energy/document/384606/download). Treatment of delivered energy: NESO, Dynamic Response A18 Submission Document (2025, https://www.neso.energy/document/359721/download). OpenEnergy keeps prices and volumes unchanged, converts delivery times to UTC and reduces frequency to monthly averages.

Imbalance prices

Elexon. BMRS Insights API, settlement system prices (DISEBSP), https://bmrs.elexon.co.uk/ (accessed 30 October 2026). Reused under the BMRS data licence. Contains BMRS data © Elexon Limited copyright and database right 2026.

Unit sizes and minimum loads

Danish Energy Agency. Technology Data for Generation of Electricity and District Heating, data sheet (May 2025 edition). https://ens.dk/en/analyses-and-statistics/technology-data-generation-electricity-and-district-heating (accessed 10 October 2026). Licensed under CC BY 4.0.

Start-up costs

N. Kumar, P. Besuner, S. Lefton, D. Agan and D. Hilleman. Power Plant Cycling Costs. NREL/SR-5500-55433. National Renewable Energy Laboratory, Golden, CO, 2012. Table 1-1, median warm-start costs. https://www.osti.gov/biblio/1046269 (accessed 10 October 2026).

OpenEnergy converts the 2011 US$ values to GBP with 2011 annual average ECB reference rates (source: European Central Bank) and does not inflate them; they are lower-bound costs for typical plant, not GB-specific.

The system files keep source values unchanged apart from dropped rows and columns, GB totals (England and Wales plus Scotland), integer MW and the start-cost conversion; changes are listed in data/system/README.md. OpenEnergy is not affiliated with or endorsed by Open Power System Data, NESO, Elexon, DESNZ, HMRC, the World Bank, the ECB, the Danish Energy Agency, NREL or Ember.

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
The system model's storage dispatch uses PyPSA:

T. Brown, J. Hörsch, D. Schlachtberger. PyPSA: Python for Power System Analysis. Journal of Open Research Software 6(1), 2018. https://doi.org/10.5334/jors.188.

Optimisation problems are solved with HiGHS (MIT licence).

Each data folder has a README.md with the full source, licence and known issues, and every summary.json repeats the attribution for the data a run used.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text: Install with uv sync (add --extra forecast for the gradient-boosting forecaster), then prefix commands with uv run.

docs.title: openenergy run
docs.text:
uv run openenergy run examples/gb-2019-naive.yaml [--out DIR]

Runs one scenario, prints a summary and writes outputs.

gb-2019-naive (naive_last_week, GBP)
  days simulated        363 (2 skipped)
  revenue               13,918.48 GBP
  revenue per MW-year   13,995.16 GBP
  captured spread       15.79 GBP/MWh
  equivalent cycles     464.7
  final SOH             0.9807
  forecast MAE / RMSE   6.01 / 8.12 GBP/MWh
  capture ratio         73.0%

The two skipped days are 7–8 June 2019, when the source data has a day-long gap.

docs.title: openenergy compare
docs.text:
uv run openenergy compare examples/gb-2019-{naive,ml,perfect}.yaml

Runs several scenarios and ranks them by revenue (plus any premium), with revenue per MW-year (battery-only scenarios), capture ratio and cycles.

docs.title: openenergy netload
docs.text:
uv run openenergy netload data/time_series/time_series_60min_singleindex_filtered.csv \
  [--scale-wind 3] [--scale-solar 3] [--must-run 8000]

Net load per year: renewable share, mean, peak and minimum, 99th-percentile 1-hour and 3-hour ramps, surplus above the must-run floor and, for the actual system, the price slope per GW of net load. See System analysis.

docs.title: openenergy storage
docs.text:
uv run openenergy storage DATA --scale-wind 3 --scale-solar 3 --must-run 8000 \
  --power 2000,5000,10000 --hours 4,8,24

Share of surplus absorbed by storage fleets of each power (MW) and duration (hours).

docs.title: openenergy sweep
docs.text:
uv run openenergy sweep examples/gb-2019-naive.yaml \
  --set battery.energy_mwh=1,2,4 --set dispatch.degradation_cost=0,5 [--out sweep.csv]

Runs a scenario for every combination of --set dotted.key=v1,v2 values (up to 100) and ranks them by total revenue. For a system scenario it keeps the order given and reports price, emissions, curtailment, cost and any battery's revenue.

docs.title: openenergy system validate
docs.text:
uv run openenergy system validate [--start 2015-04-01] [--end 2020-09-30] [--out backcast/]
uv run openenergy system validate --start 2021-01-01 --end 2025-12-31
uv run openenergy system validate --commitment --price start

Rebuilds GB prices and gas and coal output from fuel, carbon and fleet data, and compares each year with what happened: mean, MAE, correlation, 95th percentile and average daily spread of price, gas and coal output, and CO2. The system data runs to the end of 2025. Actual prices come from the bundled OPSD file and, after it ends in September 2020, the Ember file; --prices (repeatable, earlier files first) points at other copies. --commitment adds start-up costs and minimum stable output (unit commitment; about a minute per year). --price start compares the start price instead of the marginal price and needs --commitment. --data points at another copy of data/system. --out writes backcast.csv, hourly.csv and summary.json.

docs.title: openenergy system run
docs.text:
uv run openenergy system run examples/gb-2019-system.yaml [--out outputs/gb-2019-system]

Dispatches one GB year with a scenario's changes and prints price, generation by technology, curtailment, emissions, system cost and, if the scenario has a battery, its revenue on the modelled prices. Writes dispatch.csv and summary.json. Scenarios with storage need the system extra (uv sync --extra system).

docs.title: openenergy data info
docs.text:
uv run openenergy data info data/time_series/time_series_60min_singleindex_filtered.csv

Lists each price zone with its currency, date range and number of complete days.

docs.title: openenergy data update
docs.text:
uv run openenergy data update [--dir DIR]

Downloads the latest GB hourly day-ahead prices from Ember (CC BY 4.0, in EUR as published) and the ECB's daily GBP rates into DIR (default ~/.cache/openenergy/prices, or $XDG_CACHE_HOME/openenergy/prices). Point a scenario at the result with data: {source: ember, path: DIR/gb_day_ahead_ember.csv}. The bundled copy in data/prices/ is refreshed by scripts/fetch_prices.py.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Invalid scenarios, missing files and infeasible plans print a single error: line and exit with status 1.

docs.title: Forward scenarios
docs.text:
The system model rebuilds GB prices from the plants behind them. v4.0 adds two things that let it look forward, and v4.2 makes the links behave as they have and adds unit commitment to them:

  • Interconnector links (system.interconnectors: links): GB's ten interconnectors trade with France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Norway, Denmark and Ireland at those markets' actual day-ahead prices, instead of holding imports at their historic output.
  • NESO Future Energy Scenarios (system.fes): a FES pathway's capacities and demand for a year from 2025 to 2035, applied to a historic weather year.
uv sync --extra system
uv run openenergy system run examples/gb-2035-holistic.yaml

name: gb-2035-holistic
system:
  data: ../data/system
  year: 2025                     # the weather year: weather, demand shape, fuel and carbon prices
  interconnectors: links         # or {mode: links, hurdle_gbp_per_mwh: 5, availability: 1.0}
  commitment: true               # start-up costs and minimum stable output (marginal price)
  fes:
    pathway: Holistic Transition # also Electric Engagement, Hydrogen Evolution, Falling Behind,
                                 # Ten Year Forecast (FES 2025) and Ten Year Outlook (2026)
    year: 2035                   # 2025 to 2035, not before the weather year
    battery_efficiency: 0.85     # round trip; FES publishes none (stated assumption)
    ldes_efficiency: 0.75        # round trip for new long-duration storage (stated assumption)
battery: {power_mw: 1, energy_mwh: 2}

Results are "this fleet and demand in 2025's weather and markets", not price forecasts: FES publishes no fuel or carbon price paths, so the weather year keeps its own.

docs.title: Interconnector links
docs.text:
Each built link in NESO's Interconnector Register is a price taker on GB's single bus: it imports up to its import capacity whenever GB's price is above the neighbour's actual day-ahead price (Ember, converted at ECB rates) plus a hurdle, and exports when GB's price is below the neighbour's minus the hurdle. A link joins the system on the day it entered service, read from Elexon's flows (Nemo Link 2019, IFA2 and NS Link 2021, ElecLink 2022, Viking Link at the end of 2023, Greenlink 2025). Historic imports are dropped. Irish prices start in October 2018, so links need a year from 2019. Links work with the merit order, PyPSA (when storage is added) and unit commitment.

Setting Default Meaning mode fixed fixed: historic imports (as before v4.0); links: price-taking links hurdle_gbp_per_mwh 0 added to import prices and taken off export prices availability flows flows: each link's import and export share fitted from its actual flows (below); gap: a share that grows with the price gap, fitted from hourly flows (below); a number from 0 to 1 applies to every link prices prices/europe_day_ahead_ember.csv next to data neighbours' hourly prices

docs.title: Checked against history
docs.text:
examples/interconnector_check.py solves each year four ways and compares with GB's actual day-ahead price and the actual flows (Elexon FUELHH): historic imports (fixed); links at full capacity (full, the v4.0 and v4.1 default); links at their fitted availability (links, the default from v4.2); and that with unit commitment (UC, marginal price). Prices in £/MWh, flows in TWh:

The mean is within £2 of actual in 2019–2020, above it by £6–23 in 2023–2025 and well below it in 2021–2022 (see the system model).

docs.title: Link availability
docs.text: scripts/fit_interconnector_availability.py sets each link's import and export availability to the energy it actually moved over what a price taker at full capacity would have moved on actual GB and neighbour prices, 2019–2025, capped at 1 (see Data). Fitted only on flows, never on prices. Fitted on 2019–2022 instead, it gives 36.9 TWh of imports in 2024 against 43.9 actual (66.0 at full capacity), and 11.8 TWh of exports against 10.6. It is one number per link and direction, so it does not respond to the size of the price gap.

docs.title: Availability by price gap (v5.0)
docs.text:
Real links trade more of a bigger gap. From hourly flows (Elexon, 2019–2025) and actual prices, availability: gap takes each link's share of capacity in hours whose gap was £0–5, £5–10, £10–20, £20–40, £40–80 and over £80/MWh, made non-decreasing so each link can be offered as six steps, the k-th at the neighbour's price plus the bin's lower edge. Nemo Link, for example, imports 49% of its capacity at gaps under £5 and 90% above £80; IFA2 exports 12% and 78%. The Irish links barely respond. The shares are in data/system/interconnector_gap_availability.csv.

Tested the same way as the flat share (both fitted on 2019–2022 flows and actual prices, links in service before 2023), it follows the hour-to-hour flows a little better and the yearly energy a little worse:

Year Imports: actual / gap / flat Exports: actual / gap / flat Hourly correlation with actual flow: gap / flat 2023 33.5 / 24.4 / 26.7 10.1 / 8.0 / 10.0 0.47 / 0.43 2024 38.9 / 29.1 / 30.2 9.2 / 6.0 / 7.1 0.41 / 0.37 2025 38.9 / 28.6 / 29.3 9.5 / 6.2 / 7.4 0.46 / 0.43

In the model (links and unit commitment, 2023–2025) it moves the mean by under £1/MWh, lowers the daily spread by 0.3 to 2.0 (2025: 50.0 against 52.0), cuts exports by a fifth to a quarter, and changes the battery's perfect-foresight value by −7% to −2% (planning on last week's prices it earns 6% to 26% more). Because it does not beat the flat share out of sample, flows stays the default and gap is an option. It matters most for the FES pathways below, where links are short at scarcity.

docs.title: Marginal or start price
docs.text:
With links and commitment, the marginal price is closer to history than the start price in 2023, 2024 and 2025 on the mean, the daily spread, the hour-to-hour change and battery value; the start price holds the night up at a running unit's cost plus its start cost. The scenarios below use the marginal price. This is a choice between two un-fitted definitions made on history. A 1 MW / 2 MWh battery (95% each way, £5/MWh wear), GBP per MW-year, last week's prices / perfect foresight:

Year Actual Links Links + UC, marginal Links + UC, start 2023 36,075 / 45,748 1,765 / 11,838 8,660 / 28,350 3,974 / 20,397 2024 29,148 / 39,430 1,648 / 10,694 9,538 / 26,798 5,108 / 17,411 2025 36,148 / 44,927 949 / 10,413 11,623 / 26,483 4,864 / 16,955

With perfect foresight the model now gives 59% to 68% of the actual value; planning on last week's prices, 24% to 33%.

A hurdle (hurdle_gbp_per_mwh) is still available but left at 0.

docs.title: FES pathways
docs.text:
system.fes scales the weather year's system by the ratio of the FES year to the weather year in the same pathway, so every half-hour keeps its weather and demand shape:

Weather-year input Scaled by FES (target year / weather year) Wind (transmission and embedded) Offshore Wind + Onshore Wind capacity Solar Solar PV capacity Nuclear, hydro Nuclear; Hydro capacity Biomass Biomass + CCS Biomass capacity CCGT and peaking capacity (DUKES) Gas + CCS Gas + Hydrogen capacity Coal none (set to 0) Demand ED1 annual system demand Interconnector capacity Interconnectors capacity Batteries added in full: FES GW, hours = GWh / GW Long-duration storage added: FES increase over the weather year (GW, GWh)

Pumped storage keeps its historic output. Hydrogen and CCS gas plant are costed as gas, because there is no open cost data for them. The weather year has to be a year the FES edition covers: from 2024 for FES 2025, from 2025 for the Ten Year Outlook. Any scale or capacity_mw you set overrides the FES value.

docs.text:
The same 1 MW / 2 MWh battery (95% each way, £5/MWh wear) on 358 days of each modelled year, GBP per MW-year:

Prices Last week's prices Perfect foresight Actual 2025 36,148 44,927 Model 2025, links + commitment 11,623 26,483 Holistic Transition 2030 / 2035 9,649 / 10,019 27,434 / 64,033 Electric Engagement 2030 / 2035 4,853 / 14,261 22,640 / 70,217 Hydrogen Evolution 2030 / 2035 6,318 / 12,138 18,393 / 47,247 Falling Behind 2030 / 2035 3,892 / 4,311 12,106 / 16,368 Ten Year Forecast 2030 / 2035 3,297 / 3,535 13,665 / 12,928 Ten Year Outlook 2030 / 2035 2,528 / 4,259 9,967 / 19,929

Compare pathways with the model's own 2025, not with actual 2025: on modelled 2025 prices the battery's perfect-foresight value is 59% of its actual value, and the model's daily spread is 77% of the real one. Against that baseline, perfect-foresight value is 48% to 62% lower in Falling Behind 2030, the Ten Year Forecast and the Ten Year Outlook 2030, 15% to 38% lower in Electric Engagement and Hydrogen Evolution 2030, Falling Behind 2035 and the Ten Year Outlook 2035, and about the same in Holistic Transition 2030. The three 2035 pathways that rise far above it (Holistic Transition, Electric Engagement and Hydrogen Evolution, 1.8 to 2.7 times) get most of that from the lost-load days above: with perfect foresight over the full year, those days earn £49.4k of Holistic Transition's £63.1k, £54.2k of Electric Engagement's £69.2k and £30.7k of Hydrogen Evolution's £46.8k. Without lost-load days every pathway would be below the 2025 baseline: the six pathways with lost load earn £11.6k to £16.1k on their other days. A value that rests on a few days of lost load in one weather year is not a robust result. Planning on last week's prices keeps 16% to 35% of the perfect-foresight value, against 80% on actual 2025 prices and 44% on the model's own 2025.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One GB bus: no constraint between Scotland and England, which is where much FES curtailment happens.
  • Links take the neighbours' actual prices for the weather year, so neighbours do not respond to GB, and their 2030s fleets are not modelled. New links are not added as new neighbours; FES interconnector growth scales the existing ten.
  • Capacities from the register are today's; earlier limits on Moyle, IFA and BritNed are not modelled separately, only through each link's fitted availability (see Data).
  • Each link's availability is one number per direction for every hour and year (with availability: gap, one per price-gap bin); new FES capacity gets the existing links' shares.
  • Ember gives one price for Norway and one for Denmark; GB's links land in southern Norway and western Denmark.
  • The weather year's fuel and carbon prices are kept; storage efficiencies for FES batteries and long-duration storage are stated assumptions.
  • With unit commitment (the published scenarios), storage is planned one day at a time seeing 24 hours ahead; without it, with perfect foresight over the year.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
openenergy report turns saved outputs into one HTML file of charts and tables. It reads what the other commands wrote, so nothing is re-run and any past run can be reported.

uv sync --extra report      # or: pip install 'openenergy[report]'  (plotly)
uv run openenergy run examples/gb-2019-naive.yaml --out outputs/naive
uv run openenergy run examples/gb-2019-perfect.yaml --out outputs/perfect
uv run openenergy report outputs/naive outputs/perfect -o outputs/report.html

See the example report for GB 2019 (a battery on real prices and the system model), built from the bundled data when these docs are built.

docs.title: What goes in
docs.text:
Input Written by Sections A run directory openenergy run Key figures; cumulative revenue against perfect foresight; revenue by month; average day; stored energy by day and hour; price and forecast; forecast error by hour; revenue by market, plant output and emissions where the run has them A system directory openenergy system run Key figures; generation by month; price duration curve; mean price by hour; curtailment and emissions by month; battery figures when present A backcast directory openenergy system validate --out The per-year table; model and actual price by hour and by month; duration curves; gas and coal by year A sweep CSV openenergy sweep --out Results table; ranking; revenue per MW-year against each swept setting

The kind is detected from the files. Several run directories also get a comparison section (key figures side by side and cumulative revenue on one chart), as do several system directories (duration curves and price by hour together).

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default Meaning -o, --out report.html File to write --title OpenEnergy report Title at the top of the page --cdn off Load plotly.js from its CDN: about 0.4 MB per chart instead of a 5 MB self-contained file, but the report then needs internet to show charts

By default the report is self-contained and opens offline. Charts are interactive: zoom, pan, hide a series by clicking its legend entry, or save a chart as PNG from its toolbar.

docs.title: Numbers and sources
docs.text: Key figures come from each run's summary.json exactly as written, so they match what the command printed. Each section repeats the run's notes and data attribution, and the footer states the licences; share the report with those intact. openenergy run also writes benchmark_daily.csv, the perfect-foresight benchmark by day, which the revenue chart uses.

docs.title: In Python
docs.text:
The charts are plain functions from pandas to plotly figures, so they work in notebooks and apps too:

from openenergy.report import build_report, load_output
from openenergy.report import figures

run = load_output("outputs/naive")
figures.state_of_charge(run.intervals).show()
html = build_report([run], title="Naive 2019")

docs.title: Research with the Python API
docs.text: Every step of a scenario is a plain function, so experiments that do not fit a YAML file are a few lines of Python.

docs.title: How much is a better forecast worth?
docs.text:
examples/forecast_error_sweep.py adds Gaussian error of increasing size to the actual 2019 GB prices and measures the share of perfect-foresight revenue a 1 MW / 2 MWh battery keeps:

raw = OPSDCsvSource(DATA).prices("GB_GBN", date(2019, 1, 1), date(2019, 12, 31))
prices, _ = fill_gaps(raw, max_gap_hours=2)
battery = BatterySpec(power_mw=1, energy_mwh=2)
config = BacktestConfig(dispatch=DispatchConfig(degradation_cost=5))
benchmark = run_backtest(battery, prices, PerfectForesight(prices), config)

for error_std in (0.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0):
    forecaster = NoisyForesight(prices, error_std=error_std, seed=1)
    summary = summarise(run_backtest(battery, prices, forecaster, config), benchmark)
Error std (GBP/MWh) Revenue (GBP) Capture Cycles 0 19,235 100.0% 468 2 18,846 98.0% 494 5 17,261 89.7% 602 10 10,626 55.2% 903 20 −164 −0.9% 1,309

Beyond about £5/MWh of error the optimiser starts trading noise: cycles double and revenue collapses. The noise here is independent hour to hour, which is harsher than real forecast errors; a correlated error model is a natural next experiment.

docs.title: Do solar and wind earn the average price?
docs.text:
openenergy capture compares what each technology earned per MWh with the plain average price, per year:

Year Solar capture rate Wind capture rate 2015 105.9% 96.4% 2016 94.2% 96.3% 2017 93.8% 99.5% 2018 98.3% 99.2% 2019 96.1% 98.1%

In GB day-ahead prices up to 2019, neither technology was heavily cannibalised: both earned within about 6% of baseload, and almost no output fell in negative-price hours (GB had only 81 such hours in the whole extract). Solar's 2015 premium reflects output coinciding with daytime peaks. OPSD's solar capacity factors run high because reported capacity lags new build (see Data), which affects capacity factor but not capture rate.

docs.title: How big should a shared connection be?
docs.text:
examples/colocation_grid_sweep.py puts 10 MW of solar and a 5 MW / 10 MWh battery behind one connection of increasing size and compares each with the same assets on separate connections (15 MW in total), for GB 2019 with last week's prices:

Shared limit (MW) Site (GBP) Separate (GBP) Difference 5.0 590,250 618,231 −27,981 7.0 615,736 618,231 −2,494 10.0 618,208 618,231 −23 12.5 618,236 618,231 5 15.0 618,249 618,231 18

A battery added behind the solar farm's own 10 MW connection gives up only £23 a year: solar output and battery discharge rarely need the connection at the same time. Shrinking the shared connection below the plant's capacity starts to cost real money, so the saving on connection capacity has to exceed these figures. Plans use actual solar output, so these are upper bounds.

docs.title: Is planning under price uncertainty worth it?
docs.text:
examples/stochastic_value.py plans each day at noon the day before in four ways and settles every plan at actual GB prices (Ember). The scenarios are last week's prices plus each of that forecast's daily errors over the last 28 days. Revenue is after a £5/MWh wear cost, for a 1 MW / 2 MWh battery:

Year Plan Revenue (£) vs forecast Loss days 2019 One forecast (last week) 4,635 83 2019 Scenario mean (risk-neutral) 4,315 −6.9% 90 2019 Half CVaR (worst 10%) 3,412 −26.4% 78 2019 Full CVaR 2,221 −52.1% 63 2019 One forecast, one day lookahead 6,400 +38.1% 83 2022 One forecast 64,602 9 2022 Scenario mean 62,100 −3.9% 12 2022 Half CVaR 50,311 −22.1% 34 2022 Full CVaR 40,613 −37.1% 40 2022 One forecast, one day lookahead 71,213 +10.2% 43 2024 One forecast 17,633 34 2024 Scenario mean 16,927 −4.0% 45 2024 Half CVaR 12,163 −31.0% 43 2024 Full CVaR 8,873 −49.7% 44 2024 One forecast, one day lookahead 21,171 +20.1% 46

What this shows:

  • A risk-neutral scenario plan is just another forecast. The plan is fixed before prices clear and paid at actual prices, so revenue is linear in price: the expected revenue of any plan is its revenue at the mean scenario, and the best plan over the scenarios is the best plan for their mean. These scenarios shift last week's prices by their recent average error, which made the forecast slightly worse every year. With only a day-ahead market, the value of the stochastic solution is zero by construction. A prototype that also re-planned the next day per scenario (two-stage, not part of the example) gained under £1 a year over the same two-day plan on the mean scenario.
  • Risk aversion costs revenue and does not reliably cut bad days. Weighting the worst 10% of scenarios (CVaR) loses 22–52% of revenue; in 2022 it more than tripled the days with a loss.
  • A longer horizon pays. Planning today with tomorrow's forecast, rather than returning to the same charge every midnight, adds 10–38% after wear cost. Loss days rise because a day that fills the battery for tomorrow books the cost today and the revenue tomorrow.

The lookahead across all years, with examples/gb-2022-naive.yaml (last week's prices, £5/MWh wear cost in the plan) and dispatch.lookahead_days set; revenue per MW-year before wear cost, perfect foresight with the same lookahead:

Year Revenue, 0 days 1 day Change Capture, 0 days 1 day Cycles, 0 days 1 day 2017 20,682 22,356 +8.1% 78.8% 80.6% 526 524 2018 18,889 20,567 +8.9% 74.4% 76.5% 529 526 2019 13,936 15,827 +13.6% 71.3% 74.7% 468 474 2020 17,155 19,661 +14.6% 76.7% 80.5% 419 428 2021 74,172 78,277 +5.5% 83.1% 84.8% 620 600 2022 76,940 82,938 +7.8% 75.0% 76.8% 661 627 2023 35,964 40,091 +11.5% 78.2% 81.5% 612 585 2024 28,677 31,864 +11.1% 73.8% 76.9% 569 551 2025 35,861 38,936 +8.6% 80.5% 82.7% 571 547

One day of lookahead adds 5.5–14.6% revenue every year, and from 2021 does so with fewer cycles. Two or three days change revenue by under £20 a year: last week's prices say little about the day after tomorrow.

Uncertainty could matter when a later decision can react to prices, such as balancing or frequency response. Revenue stacking checks both: response availability is also committed before its price is known, so the same argument applies; balancing does give the battery a later decision, but it pays only with an imbalance-price forecast that open data does not provide. The lookahead is a scenario setting, dispatch.lookahead_days.

docs.text:

docs.title: Revenue stacking
docs.text: A GB battery can sell more than day-ahead trading. OpenEnergy v3.5 adds the frequency response services NESO buys every day, co-optimised with trading in the same plan, and measures what the imbalance (balancing) price is worth with the information open data gives.

docs.title: Frequency response
docs.text:
NESO buys three dynamic response services, each in a low direction (export when frequency falls) and a high direction (import when it rises), by day-ahead auction in four-hour EFA blocks:

Service Codes Responds Energy held Dynamic Containment DCL, DCH mostly beyond ±0.2 Hz, after a fault 15 minutes Dynamic Moderation DML, DMH mostly beyond ±0.1 Hz 30 minutes Dynamic Regulation DRL, DRH continuously beyond ±0.015 Hz 60 minutes

Add a response section to a battery scenario (reference):

response:
  path: ../data/response/gb_dynamic_response.csv
  services: [DCL, DCH]

uv run openenergy run examples/gb-2025-stacked.yaml

docs.title: How it is modelled
docs.text:
Each day is planned at the usual decision time (noon the day before) as one optimisation over trading and response:

  • MW per block. For every block and service the plan chooses MW held, constant across the block. Blocks that run past midnight are fixed by the day they start in and carried into the next day's plan.
  • Power. MW held for low services plus net discharge cannot exceed the power rating; likewise for high services and net charge. MW contracted in each direction is at most the power rating.
  • Energy. The battery keeps enough stored energy (or room) to deliver each service for its full duration at every point in the block, and, for a block that runs past the horizon, to stay idle until it ends.
  • Utilisation. Responding moves energy. OpenEnergy uses the monthly average delivery per MW from NESO's one-second frequency data and the service delivery envelopes (DC about 0.007, DM 0.03–0.04, DR 0.13–0.14 MWh per MW per hour in 2024–2025). That energy changes the stored energy, counts towards cycles, ageing and the wear cost, and by default is unpaid: under NESO's ABSVD adjustment a balancing-mechanism battery is neither charged for energy it imports in high services nor paid for energy it exports in low services (NESO, Dynamic Response A18 Submission Document, 2025). energy: day_ahead buys and sells it at the trading price instead.
  • Prices. MW held is paid the actual clearing price (GBP per MW per hour). The plan uses forecast: previous_day: the latest earlier block at the same UK clock time whose auction result was public at the decision time (results are assumed public at 15:00 UK time the day before the EFA day). actual plans on the clearing price itself, an upper bound, and is what the perfect-foresight benchmark uses.

Left out, and stated in summary.json: the battery is a price-taker whose offers are always accepted at the clearing price; it is always available and never penalised for performance; delivery follows the monthly average rather than the frequency on the day; reserve products (balancing, quick and slow reserve) and the Balancing Mechanism are not modelled.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
examples/gb-2025-stacked.yaml for each year and service set (1 MW / 2 MWh, 95% each way, last week's day-ahead prices, £5/MWh wear cost in the plan); revenue per MW-year before wear cost, as openenergy run reports it:

Year Day-ahead only + DC + DC, DM + DC, DM, DR 2022 76,940 195,927 217,004 395,148 2023 35,964 61,907 72,391 112,437 2024 28,677 45,232 47,437 51,210 2025 35,861 63,872 75,766 89,807

With utilisation energy bought and sold at the day-ahead price (energy: day_ahead):

Year + DC + DC, DM + DC, DM, DR 2022 197,160 202,931 267,469 2023 61,787 68,775 112,425 2024 45,032 56,820 79,949 2025 63,788 83,106 127,976

DM and DR start on 26 March 2022, so their 2022 columns cover 281 days, scaled to a year.

What this shows:

  • Dynamic Containment is the robust gain. Adding DC raises revenue by 58–155% every year, and the answer barely moves with how utilisation energy is settled (DC is rarely called). DC availability is 60–78% of the stacked revenue.
  • The battery works less for more. With DC, equivalent cycles fall from 569–661 a year to 319–389: holding power for DC pays more than the marginal arbitrage it displaces.
  • DM and DR depend on an assumption. DR moves 0.13–0.14 MWh per MW per hour, so who pays for that energy decides its value: in 2024 adding DR to DC and DM adds 8% when the energy is free and 41% when it is bought and sold at the day-ahead price. The default (free) follows NESO's ABSVD treatment of balancing-mechanism units; NESO's 2025 A18 document describes non-BM units as exposed to imbalance prices on it instead, and proposes to extend ABSVD to them.
  • Thin markets. DR low cleared a median 9 MW per block in 2022 and about 480 MW in 2025, against about 1,100–1,250 MW of DC; a price-taker result for one small battery says nothing about what a fleet entering these markets would earn.
  • Prices fell, then partly recovered. DC low cleared at £19.20/MW/h on average in 2022 and £2.25 in 2024, then £3.93 in 2025 (see data/response/README.md).

docs.title: Balancing
docs.text:
GB's imbalance price (the system price, one per half-hour since 2015) settles any difference between a battery's contracted position and what it delivers. It is the obvious "later market": a battery could take a day-ahead position and then deviate when the imbalance price looks better. examples/imbalance_value.py tests this on Elexon's system prices, 2016 to October 2026 (data/balancing/), after a £5/MWh wear cost:

Year Days Follow day-ahead Perfect imbalance foresight Re-plan each half-hour (t−2 price) Re-plan on known day-ahead Imbalance only 2019 355 4,417 52,791 2,682 9,152 −2,169 2022 361 64,267 324,412 60,243 82,276 22,555 2024 366 17,633 94,200 12,579 23,390 5,223 2025 365 24,693 103,850 15,916 30,993 6,018

Days with a missing price in either market are left out.

What this shows:

  • The upside is large. Knowing the day's imbalance prices would earn 4–12 times the day-ahead revenue: the price is far more volatile than day-ahead.
  • A simple real-time strategy loses money. Re-planning before each half-hour on the latest published price (two periods back) earns 6–39% less than just delivering the day-ahead position, and trading imbalance alone on the same information earns at most 35% of day-ahead, and lost money in 2019. The value is all in forecasting the imbalance price, which open data does not give.
  • Re-planning on known day-ahead prices gains 25–107%, but that is the value of knowing the day-ahead price (a battery bidding a curve into the auction captures much of it), not of balancing.

So OpenEnergy does not offer a balancing mode: with the information available, it would mislead.

docs.title: Planning under uncertainty
docs.text: v3.3 showed that for day-ahead trading a plan over price scenarios equals a plan on their mean. The same holds for frequency response: MW is committed before the auction clears and paid the clearing price, so revenue is linear in price and the value of a stochastic solution is zero. Balancing is the one market with a genuine later decision, and above it pays only with a forecast that open data does not support. Stochastic planning therefore stays out of OpenEnergy until a later market with an open, forecastable price is added.

A scenario is a YAML file describing the data, the battery, the forecast and the dispatch settings. Unknown keys and invalid values are rejected with the setting named.

  end: 2019-12-31

  eta_discharge: 0.95

docs.title: System scenarios
docs.text: A file with a system: section instead of data: describes one GB year for the system model: scaled renewables and fixed profiles, thermal capacity, fuel and carbon prices, added storage, and optionally a battery valued on the modelled prices. Run it with openenergy system run; the full reference is on that page.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
openenergy run writes to outputs/<name>/ unless --out is given:

  • intervals.csv: price, forecast, charge, discharge, stored energy and revenue per interval; sites add available output, plant to grid, plant to battery, curtailment, grid charging, net export and premium;
  • daily.csv: revenue, expected revenue, energy charged and discharged, cycles, SOH and end-of-day energy; sites add premium, available and curtailed energy;
  • benchmark_daily.csv: the same daily columns for the perfect-foresight benchmark, when the scenario is not perfect foresight itself;
  • summary.json: the headline metrics, skipped days with reasons, the number of interpolated intervals, the full validated configuration, the package version and the data attribution; sites add the co-location comparison, the plant's capture metrics, the number of clipped capacity factors and the upper-bound note; carbon runs add emissions_t, the NESO attribution, rejected intensity values and the average-intensity caveat; response runs add response_revenue, the NESO attribution and a note on what the response model leaves out.

With response, intervals.csv and daily.csv also hold energy_revenue and response_revenue (their sum is revenue), and intervals.csv the MW held for each service (dcl_mw, ...).

openenergy report outputs/<name> turns these files into an HTML page of charts; see Reports.

docs.title: System model
docs.text:
The system model rebuilds the GB power system hour by hour from public data: which plants run, what that costs, and the price it implies. It first replays 2015–2020 and checks the result against what happened, then answers what-if questions on that tested base.

uv sync --extra system   # or: pip install 'openenergy[system]'  (PyPSA, for storage)
uv run openenergy system validate
uv run openenergy system run examples/gb-2019-system.yaml

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
GB is one bus. Each hour, demand must equal supply:

  • Demand is NESO's total generation for that hour.
  • Fixed at historic output: nuclear, biomass, hydro, imports, pumped storage and "other". There is no open data to model continental prices or plant-level constraints, so these follow history (scaled in scenarios).
  • Wind and solar are free to run and can be curtailed when supply exceeds demand.
  • Thermal plant (CCGT, coal, and gas turbines with oil engines as "peaking") runs in order of short-run marginal cost. Each group's capacity (DUKES, interpolated between year ends) is derated by availability and split into equal tranches whose efficiencies spread around the fleet average:
\[c_{k,t} = \frac{p_{f,q(t)} + s_{f,t} + \lambda_t\, e_f}{\eta_k} + v\]

with fuel price \(p\) (quarterly, DESNZ), carbon price support \(s\) (HMRC), ETS price \(\lambda\) (EU ETS to 2020, UK ETS from 2021; one price per year from 1 April), emission factor \(e_f\) and efficiency \(\eta_k\). The price is the cost of the last unit needed, or the value of lost load (default £6,000/MWh) if capacity runs out.

Without storage every hour is independent, so the merit order is the exact least-cost dispatch. Added storage links hours together; then the model is solved as one linear programme per year with PyPSA and HiGHS. On 2019 data both give identical prices and costs, and a year with storage solves in under two seconds.

Assumption (default) Why 5 tranches per group; CCGT efficiency ±4 points, coal ±2 points around the DUKES average Real fleets mix old and new units Availability 0.9 Peak gas output is 80–89% of CCGT plus gas-turbine capacity each year Peaking plant costed as gas at 35% efficiency Gas turbines and oil engines rarely run Variable O&M 0 No open source; configurable

None of these is fitted to prices. Every one can be changed in a scenario's assumptions section.

Five tranches is enough: with links and unit commitment (2023–2025), the marginal price's mean moves by under £1/MWh and its daily spread by under 5% between 5, 10 and 20 CCGT tranches, while each step costs several times the solve time. More tranches only split ties, so fewer hours repeat the previous hour's price.

docs.title: Backcast: how close is it?
docs.text:
openenergy system validate replays April 2015 to September 2020 and compares with the OPSD day-ahead price and NESO's actual gas and coal output.

Year Model £/MWh Actual £/MWh MAE Corr. p95 model / actual Gas TWh model / actual Coal TWh model / actual 2015 (Apr–Dec) 38.7 40.3 6.4 0.55 41 / 57 51 / 65 59.9 / 45.8 2016 35.8 40.5 9.6 0.32 46 / 65 146 / 127 9.6 / 28.0 2017 40.8 45.3 7.9 0.60 48 / 68 137 / 119 3.3 / 20.6 2018 50.0 57.4 9.6 0.49 58 / 80 123 / 115 7.3 / 15.4 2019 42.3 42.9 7.3 0.63 50 / 64 120 / 115 0.8 / 5.9 2020 (Jan–Sep) 35.2 31.2 9.0 0.32 44 / 50 72 / 68 0.1 / 3.3

What the table shows:

  • Average prices are close. The yearly mean is within £0.6–7.4/MWh, usually a little low. Fuel and carbon costs explain most of the price level.
  • Peaks are missed every year. The 95th percentile is £6–22 below actual. A cost-only model has no scarcity pricing, start-up costs or bidding above cost, so its prices are much flatter than the market's (2019 standard deviation £4.5/MWh).
  • Coal left the model faster than it left the grid. From 2016 the model runs less than half the coal that actually ran (2019: 0.8 against 5.9 TWh). Once carbon price support made coal dearer than most gas, a pure cost ranking switches it off; real coal plants kept running for reasons outside a cost-only model. In 2015 the model runs more coal than happened.
  • 2020 is the only year the model is above actual, by £4/MWh.

These are the model's limits, reported rather than tuned away. Use it for direction and relative change between scenarios, not to forecast prices. Unit commitment addresses the flat prices; the coal gap remains.

docs.title: Unit commitment
docs.text:
Real plants cannot follow demand freely: starting a unit costs money and wear, and a running unit cannot go below a minimum stable output. So plants stay on overnight and sell below cost rather than restart, and recover start costs over short peak runs. With system.commitment: true (or system validate --commitment) the model includes this:

  • Each CCGT, coal and peaking tranche is a number of identical units \(n_{k,t}\) (whole numbers), each of size \(U\), with output between \(m U n_{k,t}\) and \(U n_{k,t}\) (and at most the tranche's available capacity).
  • Starting units costs \(C\,U \max(0, n_{k,t} - n_{k,t-1})\), added to fuel and carbon cost.
  • Each day is solved as a mixed-integer programme with HiGHS, seeing 24 hours beyond the day; units online and storage carry over to the next day.
  • Load is shed only when available capacity runs out, as in the merit order.
Technology Unit size \(U\) (MW) Minimum stable output \(m\) Start cost \(C\) (£/MW) CCGT 500 40% 34.29 Coal 500 18% 40.53 Peaking 40 25% 14.96

Unit size and minimum output are from the Danish Energy Agency's technology catalogue; start costs are NREL's median warm-start costs, converted from 2011 US dollars (see Data sources). They describe typical modern plant, not the GB fleet, and none is fitted to prices.

Two prices come out:

  • Marginal (price: marginal): the cost of one more MWh with the units online fixed. It ignores start costs, so it can sit below what a started unit needs.
  • Start (price: start): each run of a unit spreads its start cost over the energy it produces in that run; the hour's price is the higher of the marginal price and the highest such cost-plus-start of any unit running.
